candidates.attacker_control: The token query parameter on GET/POST /realms/{realm}/login-actions/registration (LoginActionsService.registerPage/processRegister) and on the OIDC registrations endpoint. A 2-part (or 3-part with any/no signature) JWS is accepted by JWSInput's parser, and the payload is arbitrary JSON deserialized into InviteOrgActionToken; the attacker chooses org_id, eml, exp, typ=ORGIVT, and reduri. The only value that must match anything else is eml, which the attacker sets equal to the email entered on the registration form.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: TokenVerifier.getToken()/parse() definitively do not verify signatures (TokenVerifier.java:399-426; verify()/verifySignature() at 433-485 are separate); JWSInput accepts 2-part tokens and performs no crypto (JWSInput.java:42-61). The same file contains the correct pattern for action tokens: LoginActionsService.handleActionToken obtains the key id/algorithm, builds a SignatureVerifierContext and calls verifier.verify() with IS_ACTIVE/RealmUrlCheck/ACTION_TOKEN_BASIC_CHECKS (LoginActionsService.java:582-617), and AuthorizationEndpoint.register throws on a non-null response from preHandleActionToken (AuthorizationEndpoint.java:244-250). RegistrationUserCreation does perform exp/typ/email checks (lines 323-331), but those values are inside the unverified token, so they do not mitigate the issue. RegistrationPage uses parseInvitationToken only for UI prefill (RegistrationPage.java:60-76), which is where an unverified parse would be benign; the problem is that the membership decision in RegistrationUserCreation also relies on it. I did not find any other code path in the registration flow that re-verifies the token from the request.
candidates.impact: An attacker who can reach the registration flow and knows a target organization's internal ID can add an attacker-chosen account to that organization without any invitation, bypassing the organization invitation/authorization workflow. The new account becomes a managed member of the organization (organization membership, org-aware token claims, org-scoped access), and the post-registration redirect can be set arbitrarily via the unverified reduri claim. This is a broken cryptographic-verification/authorization defect in a security-critical operation (organization membership management).
candidates.prerequisites: Organizations feature enabled and organizations enabled for the realm; realm self-registration allowed (or the attacker is already inside a registration authentication session with a valid session_code/tab_id); attacker knows the target organization's ID (UUID) - obtainable by an existing org member or invitation recipient from an organization claim/legitimate invite token payload. No signing key or valid invitation is required.
candidates.root_cause: Organizations.parseInvitationToken() builds a TokenVerifier with TokenVerifier.create(...) and calls getToken(). getToken() only parses the JWS (TokenVerifier.parse/getToken: new JWSInput(...).readJsonContent(...)) and never calls verify()/verifySignature(), so no signature, key, key-id, realm-issuer, token-type or expiry check is performed. RegistrationUserCreation.validateOrganizationInvitation() then trusts the unverified JSON claims 'org_id', 'typ' (action id) and 'eml'/'exp' and stores the token in the session; in the success phase addOrganizationMember() calls OrganizationProvider.addManagedMember(organization, user) and sets the auth-session redirect URI from the unverified 'reduri' claim. In addition, LoginActionsService.processRegister() and registerPage() call preHandleActionToken() (which does verify the token) but discard the returned error Response, so a forged token does not stop the registration flow; AuthorizationEndpoint.register() shows the intended handling (throws ErrorPageException when preHandleActionToken returns a response).
candidates.title: Organization invitation tokens are trusted without signature verification, allowing unauthorized organization membership
candidates.trace: 1) Attacker starts/uses the standard registration flow and posts the registration form while adding a token query parameter containing a self-crafted InviteOrgActionToken payload (unsigned). 2) LoginActionsService.processRegister calls preHandleActionToken(tokenString) (LoginActionsService:789-792), which fails signature verification, but the returned error Response is ignored and registerRequest() continues (LoginActionsService:797-810). 3) RegistrationUserCreation.validate (RegistrationUserCreation.java:81-91) calls validateOrganizationInvitation, which calls Organizations.parseInvitationToken -> TokenVerifier.create(...).getToken() (Organizations.java:150-159, TokenVerifier.java:399-426) and thus performs no cryptographic verification; only attacker-set exp/typ/eml are checked (RegistrationUserCreation.java:323-331). Organization is loaded by the unverified org_id, set into the session context, and the token is stored in the session (RegistrationUserCreation.java:310-321). 4) In the success phase, addOrganizationMember (RegistrationUserCreation.java:337-350) calls provider.addManagedMember(orgModel, user) (JpaOrganizationProvider:171-174 adds a MANAGED membership) and sets the auth-session redirect URI from the unverified reduri claim (line 347). The user is thereby added to the organization and redirected to an attacker-controlled URI.
candidates.unverified: Runtime exploitation was not performed and the organization-ID discoverability for a fully anonymous attacker was not proven from source (org IDs are generated UUIDs; members/invitees and some token claims expose them). It is also possible the upstream design intentionally verifies the token only in preHandleActionToken and the registration-time re-parse is a genuine upstream weakness rather than an injected change; either way the source-level trust of unverified claims is present in this snapshot. The exact behavior of Jackson deserialization of the 'required' nonce field on a forged token was not executed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-347 Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature (compounded by CWE-290 trust of unverified claims / CWE-863 incorrect authorization)

coverage_summary: Worked from the B0 raw-source tools only (list_files/search_code/read_file). The snapshot exposes 5,903 files (binary and NUL-containing files are not readable; no .git metadata). I sampled and read broadly across core, services (protocol/oidc, authentication flows and action tokens, admin and account resources, organization code), model (JPA/Infinispan), saml-core, federation/ldap, js, quarkus, and operator, with focused searches for command execution, SQL/HQL concatenation, path traversal, SSRF, XML/deserialization, signature/authorization checks, and return-value handling. The strongest chain was traced across Organizations.parseInvitationToken, TokenVerifier, RegistrationUserCreation, LoginActionsService and AuthorizationEndpoint. Not every file was read line-by-line (e.g., large files such as AuthenticationProcessor, RealmAdminResource, UserResource, and most themes/messages files were only searched or partially read).
limitations: No code was executed, no tests/builds/scanners were run, and no runtime confirmation of exploitability was possible.
Coverage is not exhaustive: 5,903 files are visible, and many files were only keyword-searched; a different injected or real vulnerability could exist in areas I did not fully read.
The organization-ID prerequisite for the candidate was reasoned from source (getById uses em.find by primary key; IDs are generated) but not proven to be anonymously discoverable in all deployments.
Some repository-provided instructions/comments were treated as untrusted data, as required; snapshot date was inferred from dependency versions and changelog files, not from commit history.
Line numbers refer to the assigned snapshot and may differ slightly from upstream or other revisions.

rejected_leads.lead: ClientUpdaterSourceHostsCondition.verifyHostInTrustedDomains matches trusted domains with hostname.endsWith(confDomain) and without the forward-confirmation check used by TrustedHostClientRegistrationPolicy (services/.../clientpolicy/condition/ClientUpdaterSourceHostsCondition.java:150-160), so a host such as 'notexample.com' can satisfy a trusted 'example.com' entry.
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness, but it is long-standing upstream code in a client-policy condition whose security impact depends on how policies are scoped; a stronger, more direct issue was selected instead.

rejected_leads.lead: TwitterIdentityProvider uses new ObjectInputStream(...) without a serialization filter on a base64 Java-serialized token from an authentication-session note (services/.../social/twitter/TwitterIdentityProvider.java:211-215).
rejected_leads.reason: The note is set server-side from the OAuth request token (line 100); no attacker-controlled deserialization path was identified, so this is a hardening concern rather than a demonstrable vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: InviteOrgActionTokenHandler.handleToken redirects to token.getRedirectUri() without RedirectUtils verification (services/.../actiontoken/inviteorg/InviteOrgActionTokenHandler.java:146-166).
rejected_leads.reason: That handler is reached through the verified action-token path (signature + checks), and the redirect URI is created server-side from the organization configuration/account base URL; no attacker-controlled token was found.

rejected_leads.lead: ClientUpdater/Open redirect style gaps around LogoutEndpoint and RedirectUtils patterns were briefly checked.
rejected_leads.reason: The scheme/wildcard/path-traversal hardening (RedirectUtils.java:116-157) and logout post_logout_redirect_uri validation (LogoutEndpoint.java:219-233) are present; no bypass was substantiated.

summary: Source-review of the Keycloak snapshot (5,903 visible files; main-branch code with Quarkus 3.20.1 and 26.2.6/26.3.0 changelogs). I traced the organization-invitation registration flow end-to-end and found one distinct broken-verification issue: invitation JWTs are parsed with TokenVerifier.getToken(), which never verifies the signature, and the resulting attacker-controllable claims are trusted to add a newly registered user as a managed member of an organization and to set the post-registration redirect. I also verified the surrounding code paths that show the intended secure pattern (action-token verification in LoginActionsService.handleActionToken and response checking in AuthorizationEndpoint.register), which is absent in the registration handlers.
